items.prompt: Which part of a circuit pushes the electricity around?

options.why: The bulb uses electricity to give light.
The switch opens or closes the circuit.
Wires carry electricity, but they do not push it.

hints: Every working circuit needs one of these.
It stores energy.
Torches and remote controls have these inside.
items.explanation: The battery pushes electricity around the circuit. Without a battery, nothing happens.

items.prompt: Which circuit will light the bulb?

figure.alt: A loop with a battery, a bulb and a closed switch.
A loop with a battery, a bulb and an open switch.

options.why: The switch is open, so there is a gap in the circuit.

figure.alt: A loop with a battery, a bulb and a gap in the wire.

options.why: There is a gap in the wire, so the circuit is not complete.

figure.alt: A loop with a bulb and a closed switch, but no battery.

options.why: There is no battery to push the electricity.

hints: A bulb lights only in a complete loop.
Look for gaps and open switches.
Check that the circuit has something to push the electricity.
items.explanation: The bulb lights only when there is a battery and a complete loop with no gaps. A closed switch completes the loop.

items.prompt: A switch that is ___ makes a gap, so the circuit is off.
hints: A switch has two positions.
A gap stops electricity flowing.
Think about a drawbridge that is up.
items.explanation: An open switch makes a gap in the circuit. Electricity cannot flow, so the circuit is off.

items.prompt: Why is the bulb in this circuit not lit?

figure.alt: A circuit with a battery, an unlit bulb and an open switch.

options.why: A battery's size does not stop the bulb lighting here.

options.text: The switch is open, so the circuit is not complete.
Bulbs only light in the dark.
options.why: Bulbs light in the dark and in daylight.
Longer wires still carry electricity.

hints: Look at every part of the circuit.
Is the loop complete?
Which part can make a gap?
items.explanation: The switch is open, so there is a gap in the loop. Electricity cannot flow, so the bulb stays off.

items.prompt: Match each component to its job.
hints: Think about what each component does when the circuit is on.
A doorbell uses one of these.
A toy fan uses another.
items.explanation: The battery pushes electricity, the bulb lights and the buzzer sounds. The switch opens and closes a gap, and the motor spins.

items.prompt: Ari joins one wire from a battery to a bulb. Nothing else is connected. Does the bulb light?

options.why: Electricity needs a full loop out and back.

options.text: Yes, if the battery is new.
options.why: Even a new battery needs a complete loop.

options.text: No, because electricity needs a complete loop back to the battery.
No, because bulbs need three wires.
options.why: A bulb needs two connections in a loop, not three wires.

hints: Electricity flows round in a loop.
Follow the path from the battery. Does it come back?
Count the connections on the bulb.
items.explanation: Electricity must flow out of the battery, through the bulb and back again. One wire cannot make a complete loop.

items.prompt: Choose 2 reasons why a bulb in a circuit might not light.

options.text: The bulb is loose in its holder.

options.why: A closed switch completes the circuit.

options.text: The wires make a full loop.
options.why: A full loop is what a circuit needs.
A bulb lights in any room.

hints: Think about faults: something loose, broken or used up.
Cross out things that help a circuit work.
Look for one problem with the bulb and one with the battery.
items.explanation: A loose bulb makes a gap, and a flat battery cannot push electricity. Either one stops the bulb lighting.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to build a circuit with a switch.
items: Join a wire from the battery to the switch.
Join a wire from the switch to the bulb.
Join a wire from the bulb back to the battery.
Close the switch to light the bulb.
hints: Start at the battery.
Follow the loop round, one part at a time.
Closing the switch comes last.
items.explanation: Join the parts one after another in a loop: battery, switch, bulb and back to the battery. Then close the switch.

items.prompt: This circuit has a bulb and a buzzer in one loop. What happens if the bulb breaks?

figure.alt: A single loop with a battery, a lit bulb, a buzzer and a closed switch.

options.why: A broken bulb makes a gap. It cannot make the buzzer louder.

options.text: Only the bulb stops. The buzzer keeps buzzing.
options.why: In a single loop, a break anywhere stops everything.
The battery is fine. The loop is just broken.

options.text: The buzzer stops too, because the loop is broken.

hints: Everything is in one loop.
A broken bulb makes a gap.
Can electricity get past a gap?
items.explanation: In a single loop, electricity must pass through every component. A broken bulb makes a gap, so the buzzer stops too.

items.prompt: Why must you never poke anything into a wall socket?

options.text: Mains electricity is very strong and can badly hurt you.
It would use up the battery.
options.why: Wall sockets are not batteries.

options.text: Sockets only work when it rains.
options.why: Sockets work in any weather.
Poking a socket is dangerous. It does not change the lights.

hints: Wall sockets are connected to mains electricity.
Mains electricity is much stronger than a battery.
Think about why sockets have safety covers.
items.explanation: Mains electricity is very strong and can cause serious injury. Only use batteries for experiments.

items.prompt: Two bulbs light in a single loop with one battery. Ana adds a third bulb to the same loop. What happens?

options.why: More bulbs share the same battery, so each gets less.
All the bulbs are in the same loop, so all of them light.
Adding a bulb to the loop changes how bright they are.

hints: The battery has not changed.
More bulbs share the battery's push.
Is it harder or easier for electricity to flow now?
items.explanation: Each extra bulb in a single loop makes it harder for electricity to flow. With the same battery, all the bulbs glow more dimly.

items.prompt: Draw a circuit with a battery, a bulb and a switch. The switch must turn the bulb on and off. Label each part.

criteria.label: Draws a complete loop with no gaps
Includes a battery, a bulb and a switch

hints: Draw the battery first, then join the parts in a loop.
Put the switch anywhere in the loop.
items.explanation: The battery, bulb and switch must form one complete loop. When the switch closes, the bulb lights.

items.prompt: A circuit with no gaps is called a ___ circuit.
hints: Think about a loop with nothing missing.
The word describes a loop that is not broken.
The bulb lights only in this kind of circuit.
items.explanation: A circuit with no gaps is complete, or closed. Electricity can flow all the way round it.

items.prompt: Which power source is safe to use for circuit experiments at school?

options.why: Mains electricity is dangerous and must never be used for experiments.
Power lines carry far too much electricity.
Water and electricity together are dangerous.

hints: Think about what is safe for children.
Experiments use a very small amount of electricity.
Choose the one that you can hold in your hand.
items.explanation: Small batteries give a safe amount of electricity. Mains sockets and power lines can hurt you.

items.prompt: Ines says the bulb uses up all the electricity, so none goes back to the battery. Which is correct?

options.text: She is right, the bulb stores the electricity.
options.why: A bulb does not store electricity.

options.text: She is right, only the first wire carries electricity.
options.why: Electricity flows in every part of a complete loop.

options.text: She is wrong, electricity is not used up, it flows round the whole loop.
She is wrong, the battery only pushes at the start.
options.why: The battery keeps pushing all the time the circuit is complete.

hints: Think about the shape of a circuit.
Does anything leave the loop?
The bulb changes the energy into light and heat.
items.explanation: Electricity flows round the whole loop and is not used up. The bulb changes the energy it gets into light and heat.

items.prompt: Label the parts of the circuit.

figure.alt: A rectangular loop of wire. A battery is on the left side and a bulb is in the middle of the top wire. A closed switch is in the bottom wire.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The bulb is the part that makes light.
The switch is in the bottom wire.
items.explanation: The battery pushes the electricity, the bulb gives light and the switch opens and closes the loop. The wire joins them.

items.prompt: This circuit is switched off. Tap the part that stops it working.

figure.alt: A rectangular loop of wire. A battery is on the left side and a bulb is in the middle of the top wire. The switch in the bottom wire has its lever lifted away from the second contact.

hints: Look for a gap in the loop.
Only one part can be opened by hand.
Look at the bottom wire.
items.explanation: The lever of the switch is lifted, so there is a gap in the loop. The electricity cannot flow, so the bulb is off.

items.prompt: The bulb will not light. Tap the place where the wire is broken.

figure.alt: A rectangular loop of wire. A battery is on the left side and a bulb is in the middle of the top wire. The wire on the right side has a gap in the middle. The switch is closed.

hints: The switch is closed, so look elsewhere.
Follow the wire all the way round.
Look at the right side.
items.explanation: There is a gap in the wire on the right side. The loop is not complete, so the bulb stays off.

items.prompt: This circuit has a battery, a buzzer and a closed switch. What happens when the switch is opened?

options.why: An open switch cuts off the electricity.
The gap stops the electricity everywhere in the loop.

options.text: The battery fills up with electricity.
options.why: A battery does not store extra electricity when the loop is open.

hints: What does an open switch make?
Think about the loop.
Is the loop still complete?
items.explanation: An open switch makes a gap, so the circuit is not complete. The electricity stops and the buzzer is silent.

figure.alt: A circuit with a battery, a buzzer and a closed switch in one loop.

items.prompt: A doorbell has a button that works like a switch. Put the steps in order.
hints: Start with what a person does.
The button closes a gap.
A complete circuit lets electricity flow.
items.explanation: Pressing the button closes the gap, so the circuit is complete. Then electricity flows and the buzzer sounds.

items.prompt: Choose 2 changes that make a bulb dimmer in a simple circuit.

options.text: Add a second bulb in the same loop

hints: Think about how much electricity reaches each bulb.
Sharing a battery between two bulbs gives each one less.
A weaker battery pushes less.
items.explanation: Two bulbs share the battery in one loop, so each is dimmer. A weaker battery also pushes less electricity.

items.prompt: Sort each part by its job in a circuit.
hints: The battery is the energy source.
Some parts change electricity into light, sound or movement.
The switch decides if the loop is open or closed.
items.explanation: The battery gives energy. The bulb, buzzer and motor use it to make light, sound and movement. The switch controls the loop.

items.prompt: Maya adds batteries one at a time and scores the bulb brightness out of 10. Complete the table.
head: Batteries
Brightness
hints: Look at how the brightness changes each time.
It goes up by the same amount each time.
Brightness goes up by 2 for each battery.
items.explanation: The brightness goes up by 2 for each battery added. So 3 batteries give 6 and 5 batteries give 10.

items.prompt: Tom joins two wires to the same end of a battery. The other ends go to a bulb. The bulb is off. Why?

options.text: The bulb is too big for the battery.
options.why: The size of the bulb is not the problem.

options.text: Electricity cannot flow from both wires at once.
options.why: Electricity can flow in the wires, but only in a loop.

options.text: Both wires are on the same end, so the loop never reaches the other end of the battery.
The wires are the wrong colour.
options.why: The colour of a wire does not matter.

hints: Look at where each wire touches the battery.
A battery has two ends.
The loop must go from one end to the other end.
items.explanation: A circuit must go from one end of the battery, through the bulb, to the other end. With both wires on one end there is no complete loop.

items.prompt: Leo tests if more batteries make a bulb brighter. What must he keep the same?

options.why: That is the thing he changes.
That is what he measures.

options.text: The same type of bulb and wires

options.why: The day does not affect the bulb, and it is not something he controls here.

hints: Name what Leo changes and what he measures.
Everything else should stay fixed.
Choose the thing that could change the brightness if it was different.
items.explanation: Leo changes the number of batteries and measures brightness. He keeps the bulb and wires the same so the test is fair.

items.prompt: A toy torch needs 2 batteries to work. Dewi has 7 batteries. How many torches can she make work?
hints: Each torch uses 2 batteries.
Share 7 batteries into pairs.
Count how many full pairs there are.
items.explanation: 7 batteries make 3 pairs with 1 left over. The odd battery is not enough for a torch, so 3 torches work.

items.prompt: In this circuit diagram drawn with symbols, will the bulb be lit?

options.text: Yes, the battery is in the circuit.
options.why: A battery alone does not light the bulb if the switch makes a gap.

options.text: No, the open switch makes a gap.

options.why: A bulb lights only when electricity flows.
There is a wire joining the parts.

hints: Find the switch symbol.
Is it open or closed?
A gap stops the electricity.
items.explanation: The symbol shows an open switch, so there is a gap. The circuit is incomplete and the bulb is off.

figure.alt: A circuit diagram using symbols: a battery, a bulb and an open switch in one loop.

items.prompt: Three bulbs share one loop. Rina unscrews the middle bulb. What happens to the other two?

options.text: They stay lit because they still touch the battery.
options.why: Touching the battery is not enough. The loop must be complete.

options.text: They get brighter because they have more electricity.
options.why: Without a complete loop there is no flow at all.

options.text: They both go out because the loop is broken.
Only the one next to the battery stays lit.
options.why: Electricity flows round the whole loop, so all stop together.

hints: Think about the loop.
Unscrewing a bulb makes a gap.
All parts in one loop depend on each other.
items.explanation: The three bulbs are in one loop. Taking one out makes a gap, so electricity stops and all go out.

items.prompt: A torch light flickers when Sekar wiggles the battery. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A loose connection that keeps breaking the loop.

options.why: A bulb that is too bright would not flicker when moved.
Electricity is not used up.
Cold does not make it flicker when you wiggle the battery.

hints: The flicker happens when she moves it.
Movement can change a contact.
The loop keeps going on and off.
items.explanation: A loose contact keeps making and breaking the loop. When the loop breaks, the light goes out for a moment.
